questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Anshul, Bipasha, Chaitanya, Dimple, Eshaan, Fatima and Govind sit in a straight row, all facing south.
- Dimple sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Fatima sits second to the right of Dimple.
- Only two persons sit between Govind and Fatima.
- Chaitanya sits immediately to the left of Govind.
- Eshaan sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Bipasha is not an immediate neighbour of Dimple.

Who sits third to the right of the person who sits immediately to the left of Govind?

solution.concept: Facing south: the right is towards the west
solution.explanation: Number the seats 1 to 7 from the west end. A person facing south has the west on the right and the east on the left. Dimple = 4, so Fatima (second to her right) = 2. Govind is three seats from Fatima, at 5 (seat −1 does not exist). Chaitanya is immediately to Govind's left: 6. Eshaan is at the left (east) end: 7. Seats 1 and 3 remain; seat 3 is next to Dimple, so Bipasha = 1 and Anshul = 3. The person immediately to Govind's left is Chaitanya (6); third to Chaitanya's right is seat 3: Anshul.
steps: Facing south: right = west (towards seat 1), left = east
Eshaan at the left end = seat 7
Bipasha not next to Dimple ⇒ Bipasha 1, Anshul 3
Immediately left of Govind = Chaitanya (6); 6 − 3 = seat 3 ⇒ Anshul
solution.why_others_wrong: Fatima is fourth to Chaitanya's right; Dimple is second; Bipasha is fifth. Reading 'right' as east (as if the row faced north) leads to the wrong seats.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Eight persons Lalit, Mansi, Neel, Omkar, Qadir, Rhea, Sonia and Trisha sit in a straight row, all facing north.
- Rhea sits third from the left end of the row.
- Only three persons sit between Rhea and Omkar.
- Neel sits immediately to the right of Omkar.
- Sonia sits immediately to the left of Qadir.
- Qadir is not an immediate neighbour of Omkar.
- Trisha sits second to the right of Mansi.

Who sits exactly midway between Qadir and Neel?

solution.concept: Testing both cases of a pair clue
solution.explanation: Rhea = seat 3, so Omkar (four seats away) = 7 and Neel = 8. Sonia sits immediately to Qadir's left, so the pair takes seats (1, 2), (4, 5) or (5, 6); (5, 6) puts Qadir next to Omkar. With Sonia 4 and Qadir 5, the free seats 1, 2 and 6 contain no seat that is two places to the right of another, so Trisha and Mansi cannot be placed. Hence Sonia = 1, Qadir = 2, and in seats 4, 5, 6: Mansi 4, Lalit 5, Trisha 6. Midway between Qadir (2) and Neel (8) is seat 5: Lalit.
steps: Rhea 3 ⇒ Omkar 7 (3 − 4 is off the row), Neel 8
Sonia–Qadir pair: (1, 2), (4, 5) or (5, 6); (5, 6) puts Qadir next to Omkar
Pair (4, 5) leaves seats 1, 2, 6: no 'Mansi + 2' fits ⇒ Sonia 1, Qadir 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Mansi (4) and Trisha (6) are one seat off the midpoint; Rhea sits next to Qadir.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons is not given.
- Pratik sits sixth from the left end.
- Only two persons sit between Pratik and Sneha, and Sneha sits to the right of Pratik.
- Tanuj sits fourth to the right of Sneha.
- As many persons sit to the right of Tanuj as sit to the left of Pratik.

How many persons sit in the row?

solution.explanation: Pratik is 6th from the left, so 5 persons sit to his left. Sneha is 3 seats to his right (two persons between): 9th. Tanuj is 4 seats to Sneha's right: 13th. Five persons sit to Tanuj's right, so the row has 13 + 5 = 18 persons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 17 leaves out one person; 19 counts Tanuj twice; 16 places Sneha only two seats from Pratik.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which two seats are vacant?

solution.concept: Deciding the facing first, then the seats
solution.explanation: Only the case with Kanav facing south gives exactly four south-facing persons. Then the occupied seats are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9, leaving seats 1 and 7 vacant.
steps: Seats 1 to 9 from the west: vacant, Sahana (south), Kanav (south), Mehak (north), Pushkar (south), Jivika (north), vacant, Oindri (south), Riyansh (north)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits in the third seat to the right of Jivika?

solution.concept: Vacant seats are counted as seats, not as persons
solution.explanation: Jivika (seat 6) faces north, so her right is east: seat 7 (vacant), seat 8 (Oindri), seat 9 (Riyansh). The third seat to her right is seat 9: Riyansh.
steps: Seats 1 to 9 from the west: vacant, Sahana (south), Kanav (south), Mehak (north), Pushkar (south), Jivika (north), vacant, Oindri (south), Riyansh (north)
solution.why_others_wrong: Oindri is in the second seat to her right; Mehak and Kanav are to her left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following groups consists only of persons who face south?

solution.concept: Facing directions from the rejected case
solution.explanation: Pushkar is given as facing south. Kanav must face south (otherwise only two persons face south), Sahana must face south (otherwise Mehak's seat would be off the row) and Oindri faces the same way as Sahana. Jivika, Mehak and Riyansh face north.
steps: Seats 1 to 9 from the west: vacant, Sahana (south), Kanav (south), Mehak (north), Pushkar (south), Jivika (north), vacant, Oindri (south), Riyansh (north)
South: Pushkar, Kanav, Sahana, Oindri; north: Jivika, Mehak, Riyansh
solution.final_answer: Option C: Kanav, Oindri and Sahana

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons sit between Sahana and Riyansh?

solution.explanation: Seats 3 to 8 lie between Sahana (2) and Riyansh (9). Seat 7 is vacant, so the persons between them are Kanav, Mehak, Pushkar, Jivika and Oindri: five.
steps: Seats 1 to 9 from the west: vacant, Sahana (south), Kanav (south), Mehak (north), Pushkar (south), Jivika (north), vacant, Oindri (south), Riyansh (north)
solution.why_others_wrong: Six counts the vacant seat as a person; Seven counts one end as well; Four leaves out one person.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Arpit, Bhavya, Devansh, Hiya, Kiaan and Myra sit in a straight row, all facing north. Each holds a card with a different number among 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13.
- The person holding card 13 sits at an extreme end of the row.
- Hiya holds card 7 and sits third to the left of the person holding card 13.
- The card numbers of Hiya's two immediate neighbours add up to 12.
- Kiaan sits immediately to the right of Hiya and holds a smaller number than Hiya.
- Myra sits at an extreme end and holds card 11.
- Arpit's card number is 4 more than Devansh's.
- Devansh does not sit next to Kiaan.

What is the sum of the card numbers of Bhavya and the person who sits third to the left of Bhavya?

solution.explanation: Myra (11) and the holder of 13 take the two ends. Hiya is three seats to the left of the 13-holder, so the 13 is at the right end (seat 6), Hiya = 3 and Myra = 1. Kiaan = 4 with a card smaller than 7: 3 or 5. Hiya's neighbours (seats 2 and 4) add up to 12, so seat 2 holds 9 (with Kiaan 3); with Kiaan 5, seat 2 would need 7, Hiya's own card. Cards 5 and 13 remain. Arpit = Devansh + 4 allows Arpit 13 / Devansh 9 or Arpit 9 / Devansh 5; the second puts Devansh at seat 5, next to Kiaan, so Devansh = seat 2 (9), Arpit = seat 6 (13) and Bhavya = seat 5 (5). Third to Bhavya's left is seat 2, Devansh (9): 5 + 9 = 14.
steps: 13 at an end with Hiya three seats to its left ⇒ 13 at seat 6, Hiya 3, Myra 1
Kiaan 4 with 3 or 5; seat 2 + seat 4 = 12 ⇒ Kiaan 3, seat 2 = 9
Cards 5 and 13 left; Devansh not beside Kiaan ⇒ Devansh 2 (9), Arpit 6 (13), Bhavya 5 (5)
Third to the left of Bhavya (5) = seat 2 = Devansh (9); 5 + 9 = 14
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 adds Kiaan's and Devansh's cards; 16 and 18 use Hiya's or Arpit's card in place of Bhavya's or Devansh's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons is not given; Kavish, Laila, Mohan, Nidhi and Ojas are among them.
- Kavish sits seventh from the left end.
- Exactly five persons sit between Kavish and Laila.
- Mohan sits third to the right of Laila.
- Only two persons sit between Mohan and Kavish.
- Nidhi sits sixth to the right of Kavish and is fourth from the right end.
- Ojas sits exactly midway between Mohan and the person at the right end of the row.

How many persons sit between Laila and Ojas?

solution.concept: Resolving a two-sided clue with a second clue
solution.explanation: Kavish is 7th from the left, so Laila (six places away) is 1st or 13th. Mohan is three places to Laila's right (4th or 16th) and three places from Kavish (4th or 10th): only 4th fits both, so Laila = 1st and Mohan = 4th. Nidhi = 7 + 6 = 13th and is 4th from the right, so the row has 13 + 3 = 16 persons. Ojas is midway between Mohan (4th) and the right end (16th): (4 + 16) ÷ 2 = 10th. Between Laila (1st) and Ojas (10th) sit 8 persons.
steps: Mohan = Laila + 3 ∈ {4, 16} and Kavish ± 3 ∈ {4, 10} ⇒ Mohan 4th, Laila 1st
Nidhi = 13th and 4th from the right ⇒ 16 persons
solution.why_others_wrong: Seven and Nine are off by one in the count; Ten is Ojas's own position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Seven persons Ansh, Bani, Hari, Kirat, Meher, Pavitra and Sumer sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre.
- Kirat sits second to the right of Ansh.
- Meher sits immediately to the left of Ansh.
- Sumer sits third to the right of Kirat.
- Hari sits between Ansh and Kirat.
- Bani is not an immediate neighbour of Sumer.

How many persons sit between Bani and Meher when counted to the left of Bani?

solution.concept: Facing the centre: the right is anticlockwise, the left clockwise
solution.explanation: Fix Ansh. Going anticlockwise (to the right): Hari (between Ansh and Kirat), Kirat (second to Ansh's right), then two seats, then Sumer (third to Kirat's right), then Meher (immediately to Ansh's left). The two seats between Kirat and Sumer go to Bani and Pavitra; Bani cannot sit next to Sumer, so Bani sits next to Kirat and Pavitra next to Sumer. To Bani's left (clockwise) come Kirat, Hari and Ansh, then Meher: three persons.
steps: Anticlockwise from Ansh: Ansh, Hari, Kirat, _, _, Sumer, Meher
Bani not next to Sumer ⇒ Bani next to Kirat, Pavitra next to Sumer
Clockwise from Bani: Kirat, Hari, Ansh, Meher ⇒ three persons between
solution.why_others_wrong: Four counts Meher too; Two misses one person; counting to Bani's right (Pavitra, Sumer) gives Two as well, which is the wrong direction.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who sits second to the right of Vaibhav?

solution.concept: Facing outside: the right is clockwise
solution.explanation: Vaibhav faces outside, so his right is clockwise: Lavina is immediately to his right and Reyansh second.
steps: Clockwise from Ishwar (each person's right is the next seat clockwise): Ishwar (Marigold), Prisha (Daisy), Jasmin (Lily), Naren (Iris), Vaibhav (Lotus), Lavina (Rose), Reyansh (Orchid), Udita (Tulip)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which flower does the person sitting opposite Lavina like?

solution.explanation: Lavina sits two places to Ishwar's left; opposite her is the seat immediately to Ishwar's right: Prisha, who likes Daisy.

solution.why_others_wrong: Iris is Naren's, Lily is Jasmin's and Marigold is Ishwar's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: Jasmin likes Lily and sits next to Prisha
Udita sits immediately to the right of Ishwar
Naren sits opposite the person who likes Marigold

solution.explanation: Jasmin likes Lily and sits between Naren and Prisha. Reyansh likes Orchid; Naren sits opposite Udita (Tulip), not Ishwar (Marigold); Udita is immediately to Ishwar's left, not his right.

solution.final_answer: Option A: Jasmin likes Lily and sits next to Prisha

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Akshara, Biren, Dhriti, Elango, Hansika and Jairus sit around a table shaped like an equilateral triangle: three of them at the three corners and three at the middle of the three sides, so corner and side seats alternate. The persons at the corners face away from the centre and those at the middle of the sides face the centre.
- Akshara sits at a corner.
- Biren sits second to the right of Akshara.
- Dhriti sits immediately to the left of Biren.
- Elango sits second to the right of Dhriti.
- Hansika does not sit at a corner.

Who sits second to the left of the person who sits immediately to the right of Hansika?

solution.concept: Right and left depend on the way each seat faces
solution.explanation: Number the seats anticlockwise from Akshara (corner, seat 0); even seats are corners. A person facing the centre has the right anticlockwise; a person facing outside has the right clockwise. Akshara faces outside, so Biren (second to her right) is two seats clockwise: seat 4, a corner. Biren also faces outside, so his left is anticlockwise: Dhriti = seat 5 (a side seat, facing the centre). Elango is second to Dhriti's right (anticlockwise): seat 1. Hansika is not at a corner, so she takes side seat 3 and Jairus corner seat 2. Hansika faces the centre, so immediately to her right (anticlockwise) is seat 4: Biren. Second to Biren's left (anticlockwise, as he faces outside) is seat 0: Akshara.
steps: Akshara 0 (corner, faces out) ⇒ right = clockwise ⇒ Biren = seat 4
Biren faces out ⇒ left = anticlockwise ⇒ Dhriti = 5; Dhriti faces in ⇒ Elango = 5 + 2 = seat 1
Hansika not at a corner ⇒ seat 3; Jairus seat 2
Right of Hansika (faces in) = seat 4 = Biren; second to Biren's left (faces out) = seat 0 = Akshara
solution.why_others_wrong: Jairus and Elango come from treating every person as facing the centre; Dhriti is immediately to Biren's left.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Four married couples sit around a circular table, equally spaced and all facing the centre. The men are Pranjal, Siddhant, Vikram and Yuvan; the women are Bhavika, Diksha, Gayatri and Nandita. Pranjal is married to Bhavika and Siddhant to Diksha; Vikram and Yuvan are married to Gayatri and Nandita, in some order.
- Men and women sit alternately.
- No man sits next to his wife.
- Bhavika sits third to the right of Siddhant.
- Yuvan sits immediately to the left of Diksha.
- Gayatri sits opposite Bhavika.

Who sits opposite Gayatri's husband?

solution.concept: Seating plus a hidden pairing fixed by a 'no spouse adjacent' rule
solution.explanation: Fix Siddhant at seat 0 and count anticlockwise (to the right); men take the even seats and women the odd seats. Bhavika = 3 and Gayatri (opposite) = 7. Diksha is a woman at an odd seat with Yuvan immediately to her left (one seat clockwise); Diksha cannot be at 1 (Yuvan would be on Siddhant's seat 0, and she would sit next to her own husband), so Diksha = 5 and Yuvan = 4. Nandita = 1. Pranjal and Vikram share seats 2 and 6; seat 2 is next to Bhavika, Pranjal's wife, so Pranjal = 6 and Vikram = 2. Vikram sits next to Nandita (seat 1), so Nandita cannot be his wife: Vikram is married to Gayatri, and Yuvan (between Bhavika and Diksha) to Nandita. Opposite Vikram (seat 2) is seat 6: Pranjal.
steps: Yuvan–Diksha: Diksha 1 is impossible (Yuvan on seat 0) ⇒ Diksha 5, Yuvan 4
Nandita 1; Pranjal not next to Bhavika ⇒ Pranjal 6, Vikram 2
Vikram sits next to Nandita ⇒ his wife is Gayatri
solution.why_others_wrong: Siddhant sits opposite Yuvan, who is Nandita's husband; Vikram is Gayatri's husband himself.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who plays the Violin?

solution.concept: An adjacency clue between two attributes
solution.explanation: The Piano player lives immediately below the Violin player. With floors 1, 3, 4 and 6 still open, the only pair of consecutive floors is 3 and 4, so Ilesh (floor 4) plays the Violin.
steps: Bottom to top: 1 Mridula (Harmonium), 2 Keya (Sitar), 3 Faisal (Piano), 4 Ilesh (Violin), 5 Jagat (Guitar), 6 Aarohi (Drum), 7 Hemal (Flute)
Free floors for Drum, Harmonium, Piano, Violin: 1, 3, 4, 6
solution.why_others_wrong: Faisal plays the Piano, Aarohi the Drum and Mridula the Harmonium.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many persons live between Mridula and the person who plays the Guitar?

solution.explanation: Mridula lives on floor 1 and the Guitar player, Jagat, on floor 5. Floors 2, 3 and 4 lie between them: three persons.
steps: Bottom to top: 1 Mridula (Harmonium), 2 Keya (Sitar), 3 Faisal (Piano), 4 Ilesh (Violin), 5 Jagat (Guitar), 6 Aarohi (Drum), 7 Hemal (Flute)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which instrument is played by the person who lives immediately above Jagat?

solution.explanation: Jagat lives on floor 5; floor 6 belongs to Aarohi, who plays the Drum.
steps: Bottom to top: 1 Mridula (Harmonium), 2 Keya (Sitar), 3 Faisal (Piano), 4 Ilesh (Violin), 5 Jagat (Guitar), 6 Aarohi (Drum), 7 Hemal (Flute)
solution.why_others_wrong: The Flute is Hemal's (floor 7), the Violin is Ilesh's (floor 4, below Jagat) and the Harmonium is Mridula's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Omesh, Prerit, Rukmini, Shalu, Toshi and Ved live in a building that has a basement, a ground floor and four floors above the ground floor (floors 1 to 4), one person on each of these six levels. The basement is the lowest level and floor 4 the highest.
- Shalu lives on the ground floor.
- Prerit lives two levels above Shalu.
- Only one person lives between Prerit and Ved.
- Toshi lives below Shalu.
- Rukmini does not live on floor 3.

Who lives on the level immediately above Rukmini?

solution.concept: Counting levels that start below the ground floor
solution.explanation: Shalu is on the ground floor, so Prerit (two levels up) is on floor 2. Ved is two levels from Prerit: the ground floor (taken) or floor 4, so Ved = floor 4. Toshi is below the ground floor: the basement. Rukmini and Omesh take floors 1 and 3; Rukmini is not on floor 3, so Rukmini = floor 1 and Omesh = floor 3. Immediately above Rukmini (floor 1) is floor 2: Prerit.
steps: Levels bottom to top: basement, ground, 1, 2, 3, 4
Shalu ground ⇒ Prerit floor 2 ⇒ Ved floor 4
solution.why_others_wrong: Shalu is immediately below Rukmini; Omesh is two levels above her; Ved is on the top level.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A building has seven floors, numbered 1 (lowermost) to 7 (topmost). Five persons Anupam, Garvit, Kalpana, Shreya and Yatin live in it, one person per floor, so two floors are vacant.
- Kalpana lives on floor 6.
- Garvit lives three floors below Kalpana, and the floor immediately above Garvit's floor is vacant.
- Shreya lives on an even-numbered floor.
- Anupam lives on the floor immediately above Kalpana's floor.
- Yatin does not live on the lowermost floor.

Which two floors are vacant?

solution.concept: Placing persons, then reading the empty floors
solution.explanation: Kalpana = 6, Anupam = 7, Garvit = 3 and floor 4 is vacant. Shreya lives on an even floor: 2 (4 is vacant, 6 is taken). Floors 1 and 5 remain for Yatin; he is not on floor 1, so Yatin = 5 and floor 1 is vacant.
solution.why_others_wrong: Yatin lives on floor 5 and Shreya on floor 2, so those floors are occupied.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Aadil, Chandni, Ekagra, Gyanesh, Lopa and Rasik live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Each owns a car of a different colour among Black, Blue, Grey, Red, Silver and White.
- The person who owns the Red car lives on floor 4.
- Chandni lives two floors above the Red car owner.
- Ekagra owns the White car, lives on an odd-numbered floor and lives below the Red car owner.
- Rasik lives immediately below Ekagra.
- Lopa owns the Blue car and lives above Gyanesh.
- Aadil does not own the Red car.
- The Silver car owner lives immediately above the Black car owner.

Which colour of car is owned by the person who lives four floors below Lopa?

solution.concept: Floors and an attribute fixed together
solution.explanation: The Red car is on floor 4 and Chandni on floor 6. Ekagra (White) is on an odd floor below 4: 1 or 3; Rasik is immediately below him, so Ekagra = 3 and Rasik = 2. Lopa lives above Gyanesh; the free floors are 1, 4 and 5, and Lopa (Blue) cannot be the Red car owner on floor 4, so Lopa = 5. Gyanesh and Aadil share floors 1 and 4; Aadil does not own the Red car, so Gyanesh = 4 (Red) and Aadil = 1. Silver sits immediately above Black: among the free colours (Black, Grey, Silver) for floors 1, 2 and 6, only 1–2 are consecutive, so Aadil has Black, Rasik Silver and Chandni Grey. Four floors below Lopa (5) is floor 1: Black.
steps: Ekagra odd and below 4 with Rasik just below ⇒ Ekagra 3 (White), Rasik 2
Lopa (Blue) above Gyanesh, not on 4 ⇒ Lopa 5; Aadil not Red ⇒ Gyanesh 4 (Red), Aadil 1
Silver just above Black on floors 1, 2, 6 ⇒ Aadil Black, Rasik Silver, Chandni Grey
solution.why_others_wrong: Silver is Rasik's (three floors below Lopa), White is Ekagra's and Grey is Chandni's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A three-storey building (floor 1 is the lowermost) has two flats on each floor: a West flat and an East flat, with each West flat directly above the West flat of the floor below, and likewise for the East flats. Six persons Amrit, Bulbul, Deepika, Ebin, Hamsa and Ishani live in these six flats, one in each.
- Deepika lives in the East flat of the topmost floor.
- Amrit lives in the flat directly below Deepika's flat.
- Bulbul lives on the same floor as Amrit.
- Ebin lives on a floor below Bulbul's floor.
- Ishani and Ebin both live in West flats.

Who lives in the flat directly below Bulbul's flat?

solution.concept: Flats in a grid: 'directly below' keeps the side, 'same floor' keeps the floor

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Nine boxes A, C, E, G, K, M, R, T and W are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 9 the top). Each box is small, medium or large.
- Exactly three boxes are small, three are medium and three are large.
- No two boxes of the same size are kept one directly on top of the other.
- Box K is a large box kept at position 5.
- Box W is small and is kept immediately above box K.
- The top box and the bottom box are both medium.
- Box A is kept at the top, and box T immediately below box A.
- Box T is large, and box E is a small box kept below box K.
- Box G is kept immediately above box E.
- Box R is kept at the bottom, and box C is medium.

Which box is kept immediately below box K?

solution.concept: Counting sizes against the 'no two alike in contact' rule
solution.explanation: Fixed so far: R (1, medium), K (5, large), W (6, small), T (8, large), A (9, medium). Position 7 lies between a small box and a large box, so it must be medium. That gives three mediums (1, 7, 9) and two larges (5, 8), so positions 2, 3 and 4 hold the third large box and the two remaining small boxes. Position 4 touches K (large) and position 2 touches R (medium); the only order with no two alike touching is small, large, small. E is a small box below K with G directly above it: E = 2 (if E were 4, G would be on K's position), G = 3 (large). C is medium, so C = 7, and M takes position 4 (small), immediately below K.
steps: Known: R1 M, K5 L, W6 S, T8 L, A9 M
Position 7 between S and L ⇒ M (mediums complete: 1, 7, 9)
Positions 2–4 = one L + two S with no repeats ⇒ S, L, S
E small with G above ⇒ E 2, G 3
C medium ⇒ 7; M ⇒ 4, immediately below K
solution.why_others_wrong: G is two places below K and E three; C is two places above K.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six boxes P, Q, S, U, X and Z are kept one above another in a single stack (position 1 is the bottom and 6 the top). Their weights are 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 and 30 kg, one weight per box.
- The heaviest box is kept at the bottom.
- Box X weighs twice as much as box P.
- Box Z is kept immediately above box X and weighs twice as much as box X.
- Box P is kept immediately above box Z.
- Box S weighs half as much as box U, and box S is kept at the top.
- Box U is heavier than the box kept immediately below it.

What is the total weight of the boxes kept above box Z?

solution.explanation: Weights: X = 2P and Z = 2X = 4P. From the list, only P = 6, X = 12, Z = 24 works (P = 9 would need 36). S = U ÷ 2 from the remaining 9, 18, 30 gives S = 9, U = 18, and Q = 30, the heaviest, at the bottom. Positions: S = 6; X, Z, P are consecutive upwards in positions 2–4 or 3–5. If they were 3–5, U would be at 2, directly above Q (30 kg), but U must be heavier than the box below it. So X 2, Z 3, P 4, U 5. Above Z: P 6 + U 18 + S 9 = 33 kg.
steps: S = U/2 ⇒ S 9, U 18; Q 30 at the bottom
X, Z, P consecutive; U above a lighter box ⇒ X 2, Z 3, P 4, U 5, S 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 27 kg leaves out P; 39 kg counts Z itself in place of U; 45 kg also adds X, which is below Z.

- Puneet's birthday is in a month that has 30 days.
- Shivam's birthday month comes immediately before Ketaki's among the five months.
- Dhanush's birthday comes later in the year than Chaitra's.

Whose birthday is in September?

solution.concept: Using the number of days in a month
solution.explanation: Ketaki = July. Puneet is two places from July in the list: March or November; November has 30 days and March 31, so Puneet = November. Shivam is just before Ketaki: May. March and September remain; Dhanush comes later than Chaitra, so Chaitra = March and Dhanush = September.
steps: Puneet: March or November; 30 days ⇒ November
Dhanush after Chaitra ⇒ Chaitra March, Dhanush September
solution.why_others_wrong: Puneet is in November, Chaitra in March and Shivam in May.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five persons Kedar, Mira, Sanjay, Vasu and Yogini were born in five different years among 1978, 1984, 1990, 2002 and 2005. Ages are counted in completed years on their birthdays in 2026.
- Kedar is exactly twice as old as Vasu.
- Only two of the five are older than Mira.
- Yogini was born in an earlier year than Kedar.

What is the sum of the ages of Mira and Sanjay in 2026?

solution.concept: Ages from birth years, then ratio clues
solution.explanation: Ages in 2026: 48, 42, 36, 24 and 21. Mira has exactly two older persons, so she is 36 (born 1990). 'Twice as old' pairs: 48 and 24, or 42 and 21. Yogini is older than Kedar, so Kedar cannot be 48: Kedar 42, Vasu 21, and then Yogini 48 and Sanjay 24. Mira + Sanjay = 36 + 24 = 60.
steps: Kedar = 2 × Vasu: (48, 24) or (42, 21); Yogini older than Kedar ⇒ Kedar 42, Vasu 21
solution.why_others_wrong: 57 uses Vasu's age (21) for Sanjay; 66 uses Kedar's 42 with Sanjay; 72 doubles Mira's age.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Arun, Bimal, Garima, Jeet, Nalini and Tejas each take one trip in the same year (not a leap year), in six different months.
- Bimal is the only one of the six who travels in a month that has fewer than 30 days.
- Exactly two months lie between Bimal's month and Garima's month.
- Arun travels in a month that has 30 days, and Tejas in the month immediately after Arun's.
- Jeet travels in the last month of the year.
- Nalini travels after Tejas but before Jeet, in a month that has 30 days.
- Garima travels before Arun, and Arun's and Nalini's months are exactly three months apart.

In how many of the months between Garima's month and Jeet's month does none of the six travel?

solution.explanation: Only February has fewer than 30 days, so Bimal = February and Garima (two months between) = May. Jeet = December. Arun is in a 30-day month (April, June, September or November) after May, with Tejas in the next month; Nalini is in a 30-day month after Tejas and before December, three months after Arun. June → Tejas July → Nalini September works; September would need Nalini in December (Jeet's month), and November would put Tejas in December, Jeet's month. So Arun June, Tejas July, Nalini September. The months between May and December are June to November; nobody travels in August, October and November: three months.
steps: Bimal February ⇒ Garima May; Jeet December
Arun 30-day month after May, Tejas next, Nalini = Arun + 3 (30 days, before December) ⇒ Arun June, Tejas July, Nalini September
June–November: trips in June, July, September
solution.why_others_wrong: Six counts every month between; Two and Four miscount the empty months.

In which department does the Deputy General Manager work?

questions.question_text:
Eight lectures — Botany, Civics, Drawing, Ethics, Finance, Geology, Hindi and Music — are held one per day on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of two consecutive weeks (eight lecture days in all; there are no lectures on other days).
- Geology is on Tuesday of the second week.
- Exactly three lectures are held between Geology and Ethics.
- Botany is held on the lecture day immediately after Ethics.
- Music is held on a Thursday, before Geology.
- Civics is held on the lecture day immediately after Music.
- Drawing is the last lecture, and Hindi is held before Finance.

Which lecture is held on Wednesday of the second week?

solution.explanation: Number the lecture days 1 to 8 (week 1 Monday = 1, …, week 2 Thursday = 8). Geology = 6. Ethics is four days away: day 2 (day 10 does not exist), and Botany = 3. Music is on a Thursday before day 6: day 4; Civics = 5 (the next lecture day, Monday of week 2). Drawing = 8. Days 1 and 7 remain; Hindi comes before Finance, so Hindi = 1 and Finance = 7, which is Wednesday of week 2.
solution.why_others_wrong: Geology is on Tuesday and Drawing on Thursday of week 2; Hindi is on Monday of week 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Six persons Rahi, Sona, Tinku, Veer, Wasu and Yash have different heights.
- Veer is the tallest, at 182 cm, and Tinku is 7 cm shorter than Veer.
- Yash is the shortest, at 158 cm.
- Sona is shorter than Tinku but taller than Wasu.
- Rahi is 4 cm taller than Wasu, and Sona is 6 cm taller than Rahi.
- The heights of Sona and Wasu add up to 334 cm.

What is the difference between the heights of the third tallest and the second shortest persons?

solution.concept: Turn the chain of differences into one equation
solution.explanation: Sona = Rahi + 6 = Wasu + 10. With Sona + Wasu = 334: 2 × Wasu + 10 = 334, so Wasu = 162, Rahi = 166 and Sona = 172. Tinku = 175. Tallest to shortest: Veer 182, Tinku 175, Sona 172, Rahi 166, Wasu 162, Yash 158. Third tallest (Sona, 172) minus second shortest (Wasu, 162) = 10 cm.
steps: Order: Veer, Tinku, Sona, Rahi, Wasu, Yash
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 cm is Sona − Rahi; 14 cm is Yash's gap to Sona; 4 cm is Rahi − Wasu.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A bank has two branches, North and South. Each branch has exactly three employees: a Manager, a Deputy Manager and an Officer (in decreasing order of seniority). The six employees are Bala, Daman, Joshna, Pinky, Ravi and Swati.
- Joshna is a Manager, and Daman works in the same branch as Joshna.
- Pinky works in the South branch and holds the same post as Daman.
- Ravi is an Officer, and he does not work in Joshna's branch.
- Swati holds a junior post to Daman's.

Who is the Manager of the South branch?

solution.concept: Each post exists once per branch
solution.explanation: Daman and Pinky hold the same post, so they must be in different branches; Pinky is in South, so Daman (and therefore Joshna) is in North. Ravi is an Officer outside Joshna's branch: the South Officer. Pinky's post is Manager or Deputy Manager; Daman cannot be a Manager (Joshna is North's Manager), so both are Deputy Managers. Swati is junior to Daman: the North Officer. The only post left is South Manager: Bala.
steps: Same post ⇒ different branches ⇒ Daman, Joshna in North
Daman not Manager ⇒ Daman and Pinky Deputy Managers
Swati = North Officer ⇒ Bala = South Manager
solution.why_others_wrong: Joshna manages the North branch; Pinky and Daman are Deputy Managers.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
All spoons are forks.
No fork is a knife.

Conclusions:
I. No spoon is a knife.
II. Some knives are forks.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: Every spoon lies inside forks, and forks and knives do not overlap, so no spoon can be a knife (I). Forks and knives never meet, so 'Some knives are forks' is false (II).
steps: II contradicts 'No fork is a knife'
solution.shortcut: All A are B + No B is C ⇒ No A is C.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

All foxes are jackals.

Conclusions:
I. All jackals are wolves.
II. Some wolves are not jackals.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.explanation: The wolves that are foxes are jackals, so some wolves are jackals — but that is not what either conclusion says. Jackals outside foxes may lie outside wolves, so I is not certain. The other wolves may or may not be jackals, so 'Some wolves are not jackals' is not certain either (II).
steps: I (All jackals are wolves): jackals beyond foxes may not be wolves
II: all wolves may be jackals ⇒ not certain
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

All lanterns are torches.

Conclusions:
I. Some candles are torches.
II. All candles being lanterns is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Only a few A are B' = some A are B and some A are not B
solution.explanation: Some candles are lanterns and every lantern is a torch, so some candles are torches (I). 'Only a few' also says some candles are not lanterns, so all candles being lanterns is impossible (II).
steps: Only a few ⇒ some candles are not lanterns ⇒ II impossible
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:

No nail is a screw.

Conclusions:
I. Some hammers are not screws.
II. All screws being hammers is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A definite 'some not' plus an unblocked possibility
solution.explanation: The hammers that are nails cannot be screws, so some hammers are not screws (I). The screws may all lie in the part of hammers that is not nails; nothing forbids it, so II is possible.
steps: Some hammers are nails; no nail is a screw ⇒ I follows
Screws can sit inside hammers outside nails ⇒ II possible: follows
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

Conclusions:

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A possibility fails when some members are definitely excluded
solution.explanation: The deer that are horses can never be camels, so 'all deer being camels' is impossible (I). Camels exist and none is a horse, so some camels are not horses (II).

Both conclusions I and II follow

All papayas may be bananas ⇒ I not certain

questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Some scarves are gloves.
No glove is a sock.

Conclusions:
I. Some scarves are socks.
II. No scarf is a sock.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: Some + No gives 'Some scarves are not socks' only; check the complementary pair
solution.explanation: The definite result is that some scarves (those that are gloves) are not socks. Whether any scarf is a sock is open, so neither I nor II is certain alone. But I and II are 'Some' and 'No' about the same two terms, so exactly one of them is true: either I or II follows.
steps: Definite: Some scarves are not socks
I and II form a complementary pair ⇒ Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' takes the place of 'Both' (four-option rule); 'Neither' ignores the complementary pair.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:

Statements:

No coach is a cart.

Conclusions:
I. Some trams are not carts.
II. Some trains are carts.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A 'some not' carried through a 'No' statement
solution.explanation: Some trams are coaches and no coach is a cart, so those trams are not carts (I). Trains lie inside trams, but they may all be in the coach part, away from carts, so 'Some trains are carts' is not certain (II).
steps: Tram ∩ coach is non-empty and outside carts ⇒ I follows
Trains may avoid carts entirely ⇒ II possible but not certain
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

Conclusions:
I. Some actors are not singers.
II. All dancers being actors is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Some not' passes down to a subset
solution.explanation: Some actors lie outside dancers, and every singer is a dancer, so those actors are not singers (I). The actors outside dancers do not stop every dancer from being an actor, so II is possible.
steps: Actors outside dancers are outside singers ⇒ I follows
Dancers ⊂ actors is consistent with some actors outside dancers ⇒ II follows

In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Conclusions:

Both conclusions I and II follow

Crayon ∩ brush may avoid paints ⇒ II not certain

Some whistles are not horns.

Conclusions:
I. Some bells are not horns.
II. All horns are whistles.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Some not' in the second statement gives no conclusion
solution.explanation: Bells are tied to whistles only by 'some', and 'Some whistles are not horns' says nothing about which whistles. All bells may be horns, so I is not certain; horns outside whistles are possible, so II is not certain.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Only a few tickets are passes.
All passes are receipts.
No receipt is a coupon.

Conclusions:
I. Some tickets are not coupons.
II. All coupons being tickets is a possibility.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: Four terms: a definite exclusion and a free region
solution.explanation: Some tickets are passes, passes lie inside receipts and receipts never meet coupons, so those tickets are not coupons (I). The tickets that are not passes may lie outside receipts, where coupons can be, so all coupons could be tickets (II).
steps: Ticket ∩ pass ⊂ receipts, which exclude coupons ⇒ I follows
Coupons can sit in tickets outside passes and receipts ⇒ II possible: follows
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In the question below, some statements are followed by two conclusions. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to be at variance with commonly known facts, and decide which of the conclusions logically follow.

Statements:
Some oaks are pines.
Only pines are maples.
No maple is a cedar.

Conclusions:
I. All pines being cedars is a possibility.
II. Some pines are not cedars.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: 'Only pines are maples' = All maples are pines
solution.explanation: Every maple is a pine and no maple is a cedar, so the pines that are maples are not cedars: some pines are not cedars (II), and for the same reason all pines can never be cedars (I fails).
steps: ⇒ Some pines are not cedars: II follows
⇒ All pines being cedars is impossible: I fails
solution.why_others_wrong: Reading 'Only pines are maples' as 'All pines are maples' still gives II but hides why I fails.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: J ≥ K > L ≤ M = N < O

Conclusions:
I. J > L
II. O > M

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: J ≥ K > L gives J > L. M = N < O gives O > M. Both follow.
steps: I: J ≥ K > L → J > L, true
II: M = N < O → O > M, true
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: D = E < F ≥ G > H ≤ I

Conclusions:
I. D < G
II. F > H

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: D = E < F ≥ G: the signs change direction at F, so D and G cannot be compared. F ≥ G > H gives F > H.
steps: I: D = E < F ≥ G: reversal at F → no relation
II: F ≥ G > H → F > H, true
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: W < X ≤ Y = Z ≥ A > B

Conclusions:
I. W < Z
II. A < X

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: W < X ≤ Y = Z gives W < Z. X and A lie on opposite sides of the turn at Z (X ≤ Y = Z ≥ A), so A < X is not certain.
steps: I: W < X ≤ Y = Z → W < Z, true
II: X ≤ … = Z ≥ A: reversal → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: G ≤ H < I > J ≥ K = L

Conclusions:
I. G < J
II. K ≥ H

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: Both conclusions compare a term left of I with a term right of I, and the direction turns at I (H < I > J). Neither can be established.
steps: I: G ≤ H < I > J: reversal at I → no relation
II: H < I > J ≥ K: reversal at I → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: T ≥ U = V ≥ W < X > Y

Conclusions:
I. T > W
II. T = W

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.explanation: T ≥ U = V ≥ W gives only T ≥ W. T > W and T = W are each uncertain, but together they make up T ≥ W, so one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: T ≥ U = V ≥ W → T ≥ W (no strict sign)
I alone and II alone are not certain
I or II = T ≥ W ⇒ Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' takes the place of 'Both' (four-option rule); T > W and T = W cannot both hold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: M > N = O ≥ P < Q < R

Conclusions:
I. N > P
II. R > P

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: N = O ≥ P gives only N ≥ P, so N > P is not certain. P < Q < R gives R > P.
steps: I: N = O ≥ P → N ≥ P only → not certain
II: P < Q < R → R > P, true
solution.why_others_wrong: A '≥' path never proves a strict '>'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Five statements are given: A ≤ B, B = C, C < D, D ≥ E and E > F. Treat all of them as true.

Conclusions:
I. A < D
II. E < C

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: A ≤ B = C < D gives A < D. C and E lie on opposite sides of the turn at D, so E < C is not certain.
steps: I: A ≤ B = C < D → A < D, true
II: C < D ≥ E: reversal at D → no relation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: A ♫ B, B ☼ C, C ☾ D, E ♪ D

Conclusions:
I. A ☼ D
II. E ♪ B

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: A ≥ B > C = D > E. So A > D (I) and E < B (II): both follow.
steps: A ≥ B, B > C, C = D, E < D ⇒ A ≥ B > C = D > E
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: F ✿ G, G ♪ H, I ♫ H, I ☾ J

Conclusions:
I. J ☼ F
II. G ♫ I

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: F ≤ G < H ≤ I = J. So J > F (I follows). G < I, so 'G ≥ I' is false (II).
steps: Decode: F ≤ G, G < H, I ≥ H, I = J
Chain: F ≤ G < H ≤ I = J
I: J ☼ F means J > F: true
II: G ♫ I means G ≥ I: false
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: K ☼ L, M ♫ L, M ✿ N, O ♪ N

Conclusions:
I. K ☼ M
II. N ♫ L

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: K > L ≤ M ≤ N > O. K and M lie on opposite sides of the turn at L, so K > M is not certain. L ≤ M ≤ N gives N ≥ L.
steps: Decode: K > L, M ≥ L, M ≤ N, O < N
Chain: K > L ≤ M ≤ N > O
I: K > M: reversal at L → not certain
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: P ☾ Q, Q ♫ R, S ♪ R, S ♫ T

Conclusions:
I. Q ☼ R
II. Q ☾ R

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Either conclusion I or II is true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: P = Q ≥ R > S ≥ T. Q ≥ R is given, so Q > R and Q = R are each uncertain, but one of them must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: Decode: P = Q, Q ≥ R, S < R, S ≥ T
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statements: U ♪ V, V ✿ W, X ☼ W, X ✿ Y, Z ♪ Y

Conclusions:
I. Z ♪ W
II. U ☾ V

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Decoding worded symbols, then reading the chain
solution.explanation: Decoded: U < V ≤ W < X ≤ Y > Z. W and Z lie on opposite sides of the turn at Y, so Z < W is not certain. U < V makes U = V false.
steps: Decode: U < V, V ≤ W, X > W, X ≤ Y, Z < Y
Chain: U < V ≤ W < X ≤ Y > Z
I: Z < W: reversal at Y → not certain
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II is true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: R > S; T ≤ S; U ≥ R; V < T; W = V

Conclusions:
I. U > W
II. R > U

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.concept: Combining five statements into one chain
solution.explanation: Combined: U ≥ R > S ≥ T > V = W. From U down to W every sign points the same way with strict signs on the path, so U > W. R > U contradicts U ≥ R.
steps: Rewrite: U ≥ R, R > S, S ≥ T, T > V, V = W
Chain: U ≥ R > S ≥ T > V = W
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I is true
