questions.question_text:
Here 'P ⊳ Q' stands for 'P is greater than Q', 'P ⊲ Q' for 'P is smaller than Q', 'P ≡ Q' for 'P and Q are equal', 'P ⊵ Q' for 'P is either greater than or equal to Q', and 'P ⊴ Q' for 'P is either smaller than or equal to Q'. Take the five statements as true and test the two conclusions.

Statements: B ⊵ C, C ≡ D, D ⊳ E, F ⊴ E, F ⊵ G

Conclusions:
I. B ⊳ G
II. C ⊳ F

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II is true
Both conclusions I and II are true

solution.explanation: Decoded: B ≥ C = D > E ≥ F ≥ G. B > G (one strict sign on the path) and C > F (C = D > E ≥ F).
steps: B ≥ C, C = D, D > E, F ≤ E, F ≥ G
Chain: B ≥ C = D > E ≥ F ≥ G
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II are true

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: G > H ≥ I; J ≤ I; K = J; L > K

Which of the following conclusions is definitely FALSE?

solution.concept: Definitely false = contradicted by the chain in every case
solution.explanation: Combined: G > H ≥ I ≥ J = K < L. So G > J always, which makes 'J > G' false in every case. H ≥ I ≥ J = K gives only H ≥ K, so H > K may or may not hold. L is above K but cannot be compared with I or H, so L > I and L ≥ H may be true or false.
steps: Chain: G > H ≥ I ≥ J = K < L
J > G: G > J always ⇒ definitely false
H > K: only H ≥ K ⇒ not determined
L > I, L ≥ H: L joins the chain only at K ⇒ not determined
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three are each possible but not certain; 'definitely false' needs a relation that the chain rules out in every case.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A is the sister of B. B is the son of C. D is the wife of C. How is A related to D?

solution.concept: A sibling of a child is also a child of the same parents
solution.explanation: B is the son of C, and D is C's wife, so D is B's mother. A is B's sister, so A is also D's child: her daughter.
steps: B is C's son; D is C's wife ⇒ D is B's mother
A is B's sister ⇒ A is D's daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister and mother would put A in D's generation or above; niece needs a sibling of D.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Pointing to a man in a photograph, Arif said, "This man's son is my father's only brother." How is the man in the photograph related to Arif?

solution.concept: The father of one's father's brother
solution.explanation: Arif's father's only brother is Arif's paternal uncle. The man in the photograph is the father of that uncle, and brothers share a father, so he is also the father of Arif's father: Arif's grandfather.
steps: My father's only brother = Arif's uncle
The man is that uncle's father
The uncle's father is also Arif's father's father ⇒ grandfather
solution.why_others_wrong: Father would make the man's son Arif's brother; uncle is the man's son, not the man; great-grandfather skips a generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: P is the brother of Q. R is the father of P. S is the sister of R. T is the son of S. How is T related to Q?

solution.explanation: R is the father of P and therefore also of Q (P and Q are siblings). S is R's sister, so she is Q's aunt, and her son T is Q's cousin.
steps: R is the father of P and Q
S is R's sister ⇒ Q's aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother would need the same parents as Q; nephew and uncle are one generation off.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: M is the mother-in-law of N, and N is the husband of O. N has only one wife. How is O related to M?

solution.concept: A man's mother-in-law is his wife's mother
solution.explanation: M is N's mother-in-law, so M is the mother of N's wife. N's wife is O, so O is M's daughter.
steps: Mother-in-law of a husband = mother of his wife
N's wife = O ⇒ M is O's mother ⇒ O is M's daughter
solution.why_others_wrong: Daughter-in-law would be the wife of M's son; here M is the mother of N's wife.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rekha is the wife of Mohan. Mohan's father Gopal has only two children, Mohan and Lata. Ishan is Lata's son. How is Rekha related to Ishan?

solution.concept: The wife of a maternal uncle
solution.explanation: Mohan and Lata are siblings, so Mohan is the brother of Ishan's mother: his maternal uncle. Rekha, Mohan's wife, is therefore Ishan's aunt.
steps: Mohan and Lata are Gopal's two children ⇒ siblings
Lata is Ishan's mother ⇒ Mohan is his maternal uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Ishan's mother is Lata; Rekha is in his mother's generation, so she is neither his sister nor his grandmother.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Aunt (wife of his mother's brother)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decode left to right and keep track of generations
solution.explanation: P is Q's mother; Q is R's brother, so P is R's mother too. R is S's wife, so P is the mother of S's wife: S's mother-in-law.
steps: P ⊡ Q: P is Q's mother
Q ⊠ R: R is Q's sibling ⇒ P is R's mother
R ⊟ S: R is S's wife
solution.why_others_wrong: Mother is P's relation to R, not to S; sister-in-law and grandmother put P in the wrong generation.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Vimla related to Ria?

solution.explanation: Ria's mother is Uma, and Uma's brother is Tarun. Vimla is Tarun's wife, so she is the wife of Ria's maternal uncle: Ria's aunt.
steps: Yash = Uma's husband (Raghav's only daughter) ⇒ Ria's mother = Uma
Tarun = Uma's brother; Vimla = Tarun's wife ⇒ aunt
solution.why_others_wrong: Uma is Ria's mother; Vimla is Uma's sister-in-law, not Ria's; Sushila is Ria's grandmother.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Yash related to Tarun?

solution.explanation: Yash is married to Uma, Tarun's sister, so Yash is Tarun's brother-in-law.
steps: Son-in-law of Raghav ⇒ husband of Raghav's daughter Uma
solution.why_others_wrong: Yash is Raghav's son-in-law, not Tarun's; he shares no parent with Tarun.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How is Sushila related to Yash?

solution.explanation: Yash's wife is Uma, and Sushila is Uma's mother, so Sushila is Yash's mother-in-law.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Mother's sister's relation to the child
solution.explanation: L is M's son and M is N's husband, so N is L's mother. N is O's sister, so O is L's maternal aunt, and L (a son) is O's nephew.
steps: L ∝ M: L is M's son (male)
M ≈ N: N is M's wife ⇒ L's mother
N ∞ O: O is the sister of L's mother
solution.why_others_wrong: Son would make O a parent of L; brother and cousin put L in the wrong generation or branch.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Kamla is the mother-in-law of Mohit's mother. Kamla has only one son, Ramesh, who has only one wife, Sunita. Sunita's daughter Pallavi, whose father is Ramesh, is married to Ajay. How is Ajay related to Mohit?

solution.concept: Identify the parents first, then the sibling's spouse
solution.explanation: Kamla's daughter-in-law must be the wife of her only son, Ramesh: Sunita. So Mohit's mother is Sunita and his father Ramesh. Pallavi is the daughter of Ramesh and Sunita, so she is Mohit's sister, and her husband Ajay is Mohit's brother-in-law.
steps: Mother-in-law of Mohit's mother ⇒ Mohit's mother married Kamla's son
Only son Ramesh, only wife Sunita ⇒ Mohit's parents are Ramesh and Sunita
Pallavi = Mohit's sister ⇒ her husband is his brother-in-law
solution.why_others_wrong: Ajay is Ramesh's son-in-law, not Mohit's; he is neither Mohit's brother nor his uncle.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Sameer walks 12 m towards the north. He then turns left and walks 5 m, and then turns left again and walks 7 m. How far is he now from his starting point, and in which direction?

solution.explanation: Left from north is west, and left from west is south. He ends 5 m west and 12 − 7 = 5 m north of the start: √(25 + 25) = 5√2 m, towards the north-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East takes the first left as east; 13 m uses 12 and 5 as the legs; 5 m, West forgets the remaining northward 5 m.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point A is 4 m south of point B. Point C is 4 m west of point A. Point D is 6 m north of point C. In which direction is point D with respect to point B?

solution.concept: Place every point on a grid
solution.explanation: Take B at (0, 0). A = (0, −4), C = (−4, −4) and D = (−4, 2). D is 4 m west and 2 m north of B: north-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West ignores that D is 2 m north of B; West ignores the north component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A girl is facing north-east. She turns 225° clockwise and then 90° anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?

solution.explanation: The net turn is 225° − 90° = 135° clockwise. Starting from north-east (45°), 45° + 135° = 180°: south.
solution.why_others_wrong: West stops after the first turn; North turns the wrong way; South-West adds only 180°.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the straight-line distance between T and R, and in which direction is R from T?

solution.explanation: R is 12 km east and 9 km north of T: √(144 + 81) = 15 km, towards the north-east.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 km adds the two legs; North-West swaps east for west; 12 km, East ignores the 9 km north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How far is the drone's landing point V from its starting point T, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement of the whole route
solution.explanation: V = (−8, 6): 8 km west and 6 km north of T, so √(64 + 36) = 10 km towards the north-west.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East takes the 20 km leg as east; 14 km adds 8 and 6; South-West uses the point U.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is S with respect to U?

solution.concept: Same north coordinate ⇒ a pure east–west direction
solution.explanation: S = (12, −5) and U = (−8, −5) are on the same east–west line, with S 20 km to the east of U.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: West is U's direction from S; the other two need a north or south difference, which is zero.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which landmark (other than T) is nearest to T in a straight line?

solution.explanation: Distances from T: Q 9 km, U √89 ≈ 9.4 km, V 10 km, S 13 km, R 15 km. Q is the nearest.
steps: Coordinates (east, north) in km with T at (0, 0): T (0, 0), Q (0, 9), R (12, 9), S (12, -5), U (-8, -5), V (-8, 6)
solution.why_others_wrong: U is a close second (√89 ≈ 9.43 km); V is 10 km and S 13 km away.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At about 4 pm on a sunny day, Kriti stood beside a lamp post and then walked straight towards the tip of the post's shadow. After reaching the tip, she turned to her left and kept walking. In which direction was she walking then?

solution.explanation: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, so shadows point east. Walking towards the tip of the shadow means walking east. A left turn from east is north.
steps: Afternoon: sun in the west ⇒ shadow towards the east
Walking to the tip ⇒ facing east
solution.why_others_wrong: South is a right turn from east; West would be walking towards the sun; East ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A cyclist rides 6 km towards the south, turns right and rides 4 km, turns right again and rides 11 km, and then turns left and rides 8 km. How far is the cyclist from the starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Track the facing direction after each turn
solution.explanation: Right from south is west; right from west is north; left from north is west. Net: west 4 + 8 = 12 km and north 11 − 6 = 5 km. √(144 + 25) = 13 km, towards the north-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East flips the east–west part; 17 km adds 12 and 5; 12 km, West ignores the 5 km north.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A wall clock is laid flat on a table so that the hour hand points towards the north when the time is exactly 3 o'clock. At 7:30 the same day, in which direction does the minute hand point?

solution.concept: Rotate the whole dial with the given reference
solution.explanation: At 3 o'clock the hour hand points at the '3', so the '3' faces north. Going clockwise around the dial, '6' is a quarter-turn after '3', so it faces east ('12' faces west and '9' south). At 7:30 the minute hand points at the '6': east.
solution.why_others_wrong: West is where the '12' points; South-West would be between '9' and '12'; North is the '3'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Anu and Babli stand back to back. Anu faces north-east. Babli then turns 90° clockwise. Which direction does Babli face now?

solution.explanation: Standing back to back, Babli faces the opposite of north-east: south-west (225°). A 90° clockwise turn gives 225° + 90° = 315°: north-west.
steps: Back to back ⇒ Babli faces south-west (225°)
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is a 90° anticlockwise turn; North-East is Anu's direction; South-West ignores the turn.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ravi and Sita start from the same point X. Ravi walks 10 m north, turns right and walks 6 m, then turns right again and walks 4 m. Sita walks 6 m east, turns left and walks 14 m, then turns left again and walks 15 m. How far is Sita from Ravi now, and in which direction from him?

solution.concept: Put both end points on one grid
solution.explanation: Ravi: north 10, east 6, south 4 ⇒ (6, 6). Sita: east 6, north 14, west 15 ⇒ (−9, 14). Sita is 15 m west and 8 m north of Ravi: √(225 + 64) = 17 m, towards the north-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is Ravi's direction from Sita; 23 m adds 15 and 8; 15 m, North ignores the west part.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: At 7 am on a clear day, Neha starts from point A and walks 5 km straight towards the sun. She then turns left and walks 12 km, and then turns left again and walks 10 km. How far is she from A, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Fix the first direction from the morning sun
solution.explanation: At 7 am the sun is in the east, so she first walks east 5 km. Left from east is north (12 km), and left from north is west (10 km). Net: 5 km west and 12 km north, so √(25 + 144) = 13 km, towards the north-west.
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East forgets that the 10 km west leg overshoots the start; South-West reverses both parts; 17 km adds 5 and 12.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, WINTER is written as XHOSFQ. How is SUMMER written in that code language?

solution.concept: Alternate letters move forward and backward
solution.explanation: W+1 = X, I−1 = H, N+1 = O, T−1 = S, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q: letters in odd places move one step forward and letters in even places one step back. SUMMER: S+1 = T, U−1 = T, M+1 = N, M−1 = L, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q.
solution.why_others_wrong: TVNNFS moves every letter forward; RTLLDQ moves every letter back; TTNLFS moves the last letter forward instead of back.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, ACE is written as 15 and BED is written as 40. How is DEAF written in that code?

solution.why_others_wrong: 16 is the sum of the positions; 24 leaves out E (4 × 1 × 6); 480 multiplies the product by the number of letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, 'mango is sweet' is written as 'ta po ki', 'sweet ripe fruit' is written as 'ki lu ra' and 'fruit is fresh' is written as 'ra po ne'. (The codes of the words in a sentence may be in any order.) What is the code for 'mango'?

solution.concept: Remove the codes of the shared words
solution.explanation: 'is' appears in sentences 1 and 3, whose common code is po. 'sweet' appears in sentences 1 and 2, common code ki. Sentence 1 is 'mango is sweet' = 'ta po ki', so mango = ta.
steps: mango = remaining code of sentence 1 = ta
solution.why_others_wrong: po is 'is', ki is 'sweet' and ne is 'fresh'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, GARDEN is written as MVWIZT. How is PLANET written in that code?

solution.explanation: Replace each letter by its opposite (A↔Z, B↔Y, …): GARDEN → TZIWVM, which reversed is MVWIZT. PLANET → KOZMVG → reversed GVMZOK.
steps: Opposites of GARDEN: T Z I W V M
PLANET → K O Z M V G
solution.why_others_wrong: KOZMVG skips the reversal; GVMZOL takes the opposite of P as L; TENALP only reverses the word.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, 5274 is written as 1436 and 8193 is written as 0728. How is 6385 written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap the digits in pairs, then subtract 1 from each digit
solution.explanation: 5274: swap the 1st–2nd and 3rd–4th digits → 2547, then subtract 1 from every digit → 1436. 8193 → 1839 → 0728. 6385 → 3658 → 2547.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3658 stops after the swap; 5274 subtracts 1 without swapping; 2548 does not reduce the last digit.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, LOAN is written as OANL2 and CREDIT is written as REDITC2. How is SAVINGS written in that code?

solution.concept: Two parts: a letter move and a count
solution.explanation: LOAN → OANL (first letter moved to the end) + 2 (its vowels O, A). CREDIT → REDITC + 2 (E, I). Other counts do not fit both: LOAN has 2 consonants but CREDIT has 4, and the lengths are 4 and 6. SAVINGS → AVINGSS + 2 (A, I).
steps: Move: first letter to the end (LOAN → OANL, CREDIT → REDITC)
Number: vowels (2 in LOAN, 2 in CREDIT); consonant counts 2 and 4 and lengths 4 and 6 do not fit
SAVINGS → AVINGSS, vowels A and I ⇒ AVINGSS2
solution.why_others_wrong: AVINGSS5 counts the consonants; SSAVING2 moves the last letter to the front; AVINGSS7 uses the word length.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which element is 5th to the left of the 8th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Convert a right-end position, then move left
solution.explanation: The 8th element from the right is the 15th from the left (L). Five places to its left is the 10th element: T.
steps: 8th from the right = 22 − 8 + 1 = 15th from the left = L

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many symbols in the arrangement are immediately followed by a number?

solution.concept: Check the right neighbour of every symbol
solution.explanation: Symbols and their right neighbours: % → M, @ → 9, # → A, $ → 6, & → W. Followed by a number: 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the symbols are removed from the arrangement, which element will be 10th from the left end?

solution.explanation: Without symbols: K 5 M 2 E 9 R T 3 A 7 L 6 U P 1 W. The 10th element from the left is A.
steps: New arrangement: K 5 M 2 E 9 R T 3 A 7 L 6 U P 1 W

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters are there between M and U in the arrangement?

solution.explanation: Between M (4th) and U (18th) the letters are E, R, T, A and L: five letters (numbers and symbols are not counted).
steps: Elements between M and U: 2 E @ 9 R T 3 # A 7 L $ 6
Letters among them: E, R, T, A, L
solution.why_others_wrong: Eleven counts letters, numbers and symbols together; Four and Six miscount the letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Count the consonants in the arrangement whose right-hand neighbour is an odd number. How many are there?

solution.explanation: Consonants followed by a number: K 5, M 2, T 3, P 1. Of these, the number is odd in 2 case(s): T 3, P 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

B 8 © Q 4 I ★ 6 D N 3 £ O 9 G 2 ¥ S 7 H

If every element in an odd position (1st, 3rd, 5th, …) of the arrangement is removed, which element will be 5th from the right end of the new arrangement?

solution.concept: Removing alternate elements halves the arrangement
solution.explanation: Keeping only the elements in even positions gives 8 Q I 6 N £ 9 2 S H. Counting from the right, the 5th is £.
steps: Even positions: 8 Q I 6 N £ 9 2 S H

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

5 F # 8 K @ E 2 L % 9 M U 3 $ P 6 & R 4 A

How many numbers in the arrangement are immediately preceded by a consonant and immediately followed by a symbol?

solution.explanation: Numbers with both neighbours: # 8 K; E 2 L; % 9 M; U 3 $; P 6 &; R 4 A. Consonant before and symbol after: P 6 & — 1.
steps: Check each number's left and right neighbour

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If all the symbols are removed, which element will be 4th to the right of the 9th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Delete, convert the right-end position, then move
solution.explanation: Without the six symbols there are 20 elements: 9 D 4 I 7 Q F 2 H O 5 S 8 A 3 E 6 Z N 1. The 9th from the right is the 12th from the left (S); four places to its right is the 16th: E.
steps: New arrangement: 9 D 4 I 7 Q F 2 H O 5 S 8 A 3 E 6 Z N 1
9th from the right = 20 − 9 + 1 = 12th from the left = S

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the sum of all the numbers in the arrangement that are immediately preceded by a vowel?

solution.explanation: The vowels are I, O, A and E. I is followed by 7, O by 5, E by 6, and A by the symbol #. Sum: 7 + 5 + 6 = 18.
steps: Right neighbours: I → 7, O → 5, A → #, E → 6
solution.why_others_wrong: 12 leaves out 6; 21 adds the 3 that follows #; 26 adds the 8 before A.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Count the consonants that have a symbol on their immediate left and a number on their immediate right in this arrangement. How many such consonants are there?

solution.explanation: Consonants with both neighbours: 9 D £; 7 Q ★; ★ F 2; © H O; ¥ S 8; 6 Z @; @ N 1. Symbol before and number after: ★ F 2, ¥ S 8, @ N 1 — 3.
steps: List each consonant with its two neighbours

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Three of the following four groups are formed in the same way from the arrangement (an element, then the element two places to its right, then the element between them). Which group does NOT belong?

solution.concept: Read each group back into the arrangement
solution.explanation: In the arrangement D is followed by £ and then 4, so 'D 4 £' takes an element, the element two places to its right and then the element between them. '2 H ©' (from 2 © H) and 'S A 8' (from S 8 A) are formed the same way. O is followed by 5 and ¥, so the same rule would give 'O ¥ 5', not 'O ¥ S'.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the first thirteen elements of the arrangement are written in reverse order, which element will be 7th to the left of the 20th element from the left end?

solution.explanation: After reversing the first thirteen: O H © 2 F ★ Q 7 I 4 £ D 9 5 ¥ S 8 A # 3 E 6 Z @ N 1. The 20th element is 3 (unchanged, outside the block); seven places to its left is the 13th, which is now 9 (originally the 1st element).
steps: New order: O H © 2 F ★ Q 7 I 4 £ D 9 5 ¥ S 8 A # 3 E 6 Z @ N 1

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every letter in an odd-numbered position of the English alphabet (A, C, E, …) is removed, which letter will be 7th from the right end of the remaining letters?

solution.explanation: The remaining letters are B D F H J L N P R T V X Z (13 letters). Counting from the right: Z, X, V, T, R, P, N.
steps: Remaining: B D F H J L N P R T V X Z
7th from the right = 7th from the left of the reversed list = N
solution.why_others_wrong: L is 8th and P 6th from the right; M was removed (it is 13th, an odd position).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If every third letter of the English alphabet (C, F, I, …) is removed, which letter will be 10th from the left end of the remaining letters?

solution.concept: Two of every three letters remain
solution.explanation: Remaining letters: A B D E G H J K M N P Q S T V W Y Z. The 10th is N.
steps: Every block of three keeps its first two letters
10th remaining = 2nd letter of the 5th block (M N O) = N
solution.shortcut: Ten remaining letters = five blocks of two; the 5th block is M N O, so the 10th is N.
solution.why_others_wrong: M is the 9th remaining letter; O was removed; P is the 11th.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words can be formed using the letters of the word 'INTERNATIONAL', each letter used no more often than it appears in INTERNATIONAL?

solution.explanation: INTERNATIONAL has I×2, N×3, T×2, E, R, A×2, O and L. ALTERNATION needs A×2, L, T×2, E, R, N×3, I and O, all available. INTERVAL needs a V, LATITUDE needs U and D, and TERMINAL needs an M, none of which occur.
steps: Letters available: A2 E1 I2 L1 N3 O1 R1 T2
ALTERNATION: A2 E1 I1 L1 N3 O1 R1 T2 ✓

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If the words BANNER, BANK, BANQUET, BANJO and BANDIT are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary, which word will be third?

solution.concept: Dictionary order is decided by the first letter that differs
solution.explanation: All five start with BAN, so compare the 4th letters: D (BANDIT), J (BANJO), K (BANK), N (BANNER), Q (BANQUET). The third is BANK.
steps: 4th letters: D < J < K < N < Q
Order: BANDIT, BANJO, BANK, BANNER, BANQUET
solution.why_others_wrong: BANJO is second, BANNER fourth and BANDIT first.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'FLOWCHART' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.concept: Compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet
solution.explanation: Pairs found: LH, LR, CA — 3 in all.
steps: Positions in the word vs alphabet positions: F 6, L 12, O 15, W 23, C 3, H 8, A 1, R 18, T 20
A pair qualifies when |word gap| = |alphabet gap|

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the word 'DISTANCE', how many pairs of letters have the same number of letters between them in the word as between them in the English alphabet? Count a pair whether its letters appear in alphabetical or reverse order.

solution.concept: Compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet
solution.explanation: Pairs found: ST, AC — 2 in all.
steps: Alphabet positions: D 4, I 9, S 19, T 20, A 1, N 14, C 3, E 5
A pair qualifies when |word gap| = |alphabet gap|

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Each letter of the word 'BLANKET' is replaced by the letter three places after it in the English alphabet, and the new letters are then arranged in alphabetical order from left to right. Which letter will be third from the left?

solution.explanation: B→E, L→O, A→D, N→Q, K→N, E→H, T→W gives E O D Q N H W. In alphabetical order: D E H N O Q W. The third is H.
steps: +3: E O D Q N H W
Sorted: D E H N O Q W
solution.why_others_wrong: E is second; N fourth; O fifth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Rohit ranks 13th from the top in a class of 41 students. What is his rank from the bottom?

solution.concept: From the other end = total − rank + 1
solution.explanation: Rank from the bottom = 41 − 13 + 1 = 29th.
solution.why_others_wrong: 28th forgets to add 1; 30th adds 2; 27th subtracts 1 instead of adding.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a queue, Asha is 5th from the front and Bina, who stands behind Asha, is 6th from the back. Exactly eight persons stand between Asha and Bina. How many persons are there in the queue?

solution.explanation: Asha's position from the front is 5. Eight persons stand between, so Bina is 5 + 8 + 1 = 14th from the front. She is 6th from the back, so the queue has 14 + 6 − 1 = 19 persons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 subtracts one person too many; 20 forgets to subtract Bina once; 21 counts both Asha and Bina twice.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Among five boys A, B, C, D and E, each of a different height, A is taller than B, C is shorter than B, D is taller than A, and E is the shortest. Who is the third tallest?

solution.concept: Build the order from pairwise clues
solution.explanation: D > A > B > C, and E is last: D, A, B, C, E. The third tallest is B.
steps: E shortest ⇒ D, A, B, C, E
solution.why_others_wrong: A is second, D tallest, C fourth.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Anu is 7th from the left end and 15th from the right end of a row of girls. How many more girls must join the row so that there are 30 girls in it?

solution.explanation: The row has 7 + 15 − 1 = 21 girls, so 30 − 21 = 9 more are needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 forgets to subtract Anu once (22 girls); 10 subtracts her twice; 7 is her position.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a class of 31 students, 6 students failed an examination and are ranked below all those who passed. Among the students who passed, Ravi is 7th from the top. What is Ravi's rank from the bottom in the whole class?

solution.concept: Failed students sit below him, so they count
solution.explanation: Since everyone who failed is ranked below everyone who passed, Ravi is also 7th from the top of the whole class. His rank from the bottom is 31 − 7 + 1 = 25th.
steps: Failed students are below all passed students ⇒ Ravi is 7th from the top overall
solution.why_others_wrong: 19th is his rank from the bottom among the 25 who passed only; 24th forgets to add 1; 26th adds 2.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Who scored the third highest marks?

solution.explanation: Highest to lowest: Kriti, Pia, Ira, Jojo, Dev, Moti, Ahana. Third: Ira.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If Jojo scored 71 marks and Moti scored 58, which of the following can be Dev's score?

solution.concept: A middle rank must lie strictly between its neighbours
solution.explanation: Dev is below Jojo and above Moti, so his marks are less than 71 and more than 58 (all marks are different). Only 64 fits.
solution.why_others_wrong: 57 is below Moti; 71 equals Jojo's marks; 73 is above Jojo.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many students scored more than Jojo but less than Kriti?

solution.explanation: Between Kriti (1st) and Jojo (4th) are Pia and Ira: two students.
steps: Order: Kriti, Pia, Ira, Jojo, Dev, Moti, Ahana

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row, all facing north. Amit is 11th from the left end and Bhola is 16th from the right end. Chetan sits exactly midway between Amit and Bhola, and exactly seven persons sit between Amit and Chetan. How many persons sit in the row?

solution.explanation: Seven persons between Amit and Chetan put Chetan 8 places from Amit. Bhola cannot be to Amit's left (Chetan would be at position 3 and Bhola at −5), so Chetan is 19th and Bhola, as far again, is 27th from the left. With Bhola 16th from the right, the row has 27 + 16 − 1 = 42 persons.
solution.why_others_wrong: 41 subtracts Bhola twice; 43 forgets to subtract him once; 40 places Chetan 7 places away instead of 8.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Class A has 28 students and class B has 32. In class A, Ritu is 9th from the top; in class B, Sonu is 11th from the bottom. The two classes are combined into one ranking list of 60 students, in which Ritu is 15th from the top and Sonu is 23rd from the bottom. How many students are ranked between Ritu and Sonu in the combined list?

solution.explanation: In the combined list of 60, Ritu is 15th from the top and Sonu is 60 − 23 + 1 = 38th from the top. Between them are 38 − 15 − 1 = 22 students. The ranks within the old classes are not needed.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 subtracts one too many; 23 forgets to exclude one end; 40 mixes the class ranks with the combined ranks.

In Step III, which word is second to the right of 'path'?

Step II: tlephane wainbor kite sun garden paper
Step III: tlephane wainbor nardeg kite sun paper

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A number machine works step by step. In each step it takes, among the numbers not yet arranged, the number closest to 50, replaces it by its distance from 50 (for example, 47 becomes 3), and places the result at the left end, immediately to the right of the results already placed. The other numbers keep their order.

Input: 37 62 49 81 55 23

What is the sum of all the numbers in Step IV?

solution.why_others_wrong: The other values are the sums of Step III, Step V and the input.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by two statements, I and II. Decide whether the data in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: What is the straight-line distance between village P and village Q?

I. Village P is 6 km north of village R.
II. Village Q is 8 km east of village R.

options.text: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary

solution.concept: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone, then together
solution.explanation: I places P relative to R but says nothing about Q; II places Q relative to R but says nothing about P. Together, P and Q are the ends of a right angle at R with legs 6 km and 8 km, so PQ = 10 km.
steps: I alone: Q unknown ⇒ not sufficient
II alone: P unknown ⇒ not sufficient
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both statements I and II together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
The question below is followed by three statements, I, II and III. Decide which of the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Question: How many students are there in the class?

I. Ravi is 12th from the top.
II. Sita is 20th from the bottom.
III. Ravi is 4 ranks above Sita.

options.text: Only statements I and III together are sufficient
Only statements II and III together are sufficient
All three statements I, II and III together are necessary
Even all three statements together are not sufficient

solution.concept: Three-statement data sufficiency: test every pair
solution.explanation: To count the class we need one person's rank from both ends. I + III: Sita is 16th from the top, but her rank from the bottom is unknown. II + III: Ravi is 24th from the bottom, but his rank from the top is unknown. I + II: two different persons, with no link between them. All three: Sita is 16th from the top and 20th from the bottom, so the class has 16 + 20 − 1 = 35 students.
steps: I + II: no link between Ravi and Sita ⇒ not sufficient
I + III: Sita 16th from the top only
II + III: Ravi 24th from the bottom only
solution.final_answer: Option C: All three statements I, II and III together are necessary

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: Notice in a library: "Books must be returned within 14 days. A fine of ₹5 per day will be charged after that."

Assumptions:
I. Some borrowers may keep books for longer than 14 days.
II. The fine will encourage borrowers to return books on time.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: A rule with a late fine is needed only if some borrowers might keep books beyond the limit (I). Fixing a fine assumes that it will push borrowers to return books on time (II); otherwise the fine would serve no purpose.
steps: Late-return rule ⇒ late returns are expected: I implicit
A fine is meant to deter ⇒ II implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one premise of the notice; Neither ignores both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The principal has asked parents to send their children to school with raincoats during the monsoon.

Assumptions:
I. It is likely to rain while the children are on their way to or from school during the monsoon.
II. All parents drop their children to school by car.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Asking for raincoats makes sense only if rain is likely during the school journey (I). If all children came by car, raincoats would hardly be needed, so II runs against the request.
steps: Raincoats are requested because rain is expected ⇒ I implicit
II would make the request pointless ⇒ not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Both and Only II accept II, which contradicts the purpose of the request.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: A notice beside the lift of an office building: "To save electricity, please use the stairs if you are going up or down only one or two floors."

Assumptions:
I. People in the building never use the stairs.
II. Using the lift for short trips uses electricity that could be saved.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The notice links using the stairs for short trips to saving electricity, so it assumes that the lift uses electricity on such trips (II). It asks people to use the stairs more; it does not assume that they never use them (I).
steps: Purpose: save electricity by avoiding short lift trips ⇒ II implicit
'Never use the stairs' is an extreme claim the notice does not need ⇒ I not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both accept an extreme 'never' claim.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only assumption II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The municipal corporation has announced that the water supply will be cut for six hours on Sunday for pipeline repairs and has advised residents to store water in advance.

Assumptions:
I. Residents are able to store water in advance.
II. Residents will need water during the six hours when the supply is cut.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Advising residents to store water assumes they can do so (I) and that they will need water while the supply is off (II); without either premise the advice would be pointless.
steps: Advice to store water ⇒ residents can store it: I implicit
Storing water in advance matters only if water is needed during the cut ⇒ II implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one of two premises the advice rests on.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: An advertisement: "Join our weekend yoga classes — the only classes in the city taught by a certified instructor."

Assumptions:
I. Everyone in the city wants to learn yoga.
II. People who join yoga classes cannot attend classes on weekdays.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The advertisement offers weekend classes and highlights the certified instructor. It does not need everyone to want yoga (I is an extreme generalisation), and offering weekend classes does not assume that no learner can come on weekdays (II).
steps: I: 'everyone' is extreme and not needed ⇒ not implicit
II: weekend classes suit some people; nothing says no one can attend on weekdays ⇒ not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other options accepts at least one claim the advertiser does not need.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The bank has decided to open its new branch in the industrial area rather than in the nearby residential colony.

Assumptions:
I. The bank expects the industrial area to bring it more business than the residential colony.
II. The residential colony has no residents who need banking services.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Choosing one location over another assumes that the chosen one is expected to be better for the bank, most naturally in business terms (I). The choice does not require the colony to have no banking needs at all (II); it only needs the industrial area to be the better option.
steps: Preference for the industrial area ⇒ it is expected to be more useful: I implicit
'No residents who need banking' is extreme; a weaker reason is enough ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both accept an extreme claim; Neither ignores the basis of the choice.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only assumption I is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The state government plans to set up cold-storage units near major vegetable markets to reduce the wastage of vegetables.

Assumptions:
I. A significant part of the wastage happens because vegetables cannot be stored in cold conditions.
II. Traders and farmers will be able to use cold-storage units located near the markets.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The plan expects cold storage to reduce wastage, so it assumes that lack of cold storage is a real cause of the wastage (I). Placing the units near markets assumes the people who handle the vegetables there can use them (II); unusable units would not reduce wastage.
steps: Remedy = cold storage ⇒ cause includes lack of cold storage: I implicit
Units near markets must be usable by those who handle the produce ⇒ II implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Each 'Only' option drops one premise the plan needs; Neither ignores both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both I and II are implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: An airline has announced that passengers who check in online can use a separate fast-track security lane at the airport.

Assumptions:
I. Most passengers prefer to check in at the airport counter.
II. A separate lane can reduce the time that passengers who check in online spend in the security queue.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: Offering a fast-track lane as a benefit assumes the lane actually saves time for those passengers (II). The airline need not assume anything about what most passengers prefer (I); if anything, the offer hopes to move more passengers to online check-in.
steps: Benefit offered = shorter security wait ⇒ II implicit
Preference of 'most passengers' is not needed for the offer ⇒ I not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both accept a claim about majority preference that the announcement does not rely on.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only assumption II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two assumptions. An assumption is something supposed or taken for granted by the person making the statement. Decide which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement.

Statement: The city's mayor said, "The new cycle lanes have been a success: the number of people cycling on the main roads has doubled since they opened."

Assumptions:
I. Before the cycle lanes opened, nobody in the city cycled.
II. Every cyclist in the city now rides only on the cycle lanes.

options.text: Neither I nor II is implicit
Both I and II are implicit

solution.concept: Implicit assumption: what the speaker must take for granted
solution.explanation: The mayor assumes that the rise in cycling is due to the lanes, but neither assumption says that. 'Doubled' means there were cyclists before, so I contradicts the statement; II is an extreme claim about every cyclist that the mayor's success claim does not need.
steps: 'Doubled' implies some cyclists before ⇒ I contradicts the statement
'Every cyclist only on the lanes' is extreme and unnecessary ⇒ II not implicit
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options accept at least one claim the statement either contradicts or does not need.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither I nor II is implicit

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: All trains that leave from platform 3 go to Nagpur. The 5:10 pm train leaves from platform 3.

Conclusions:
I. The 5:10 pm train goes to Nagpur.
II. No train that leaves from platform 1 goes to Nagpur.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The rule covers every train leaving from platform 3, and the 5:10 pm train is one of them, so I follows. The statement says nothing about trains from other platforms, so II does not follow.
steps: All platform-3 trains → Nagpur; the 5:10 pm train is a platform-3 train ⇒ I
Platform 1 is never mentioned ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both rely on information about platform 1 that is not given.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The price of milk rose from ₹54 to ₹60 a litre, while a family's monthly milk consumption stayed at 30 litres.

Conclusions:
I. The family's monthly spending on milk rose by ₹180.
II. The family's total monthly expenses rose.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The increase is (60 − 54) × 30 = ₹180 a month, so I follows. The family's other expenses are not given; they may have fallen by more, so II does not follow.
steps: Other expenses unknown ⇒ II does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both assume that nothing else in the budget changed.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Only conclusion I follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Some of the city's buses run on electricity, and every electric bus in the city was bought last year.

Conclusions:
I. All the buses the city bought last year run on electricity.
II. Some of the city's buses were bought last year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The electric buses exist and were all bought last year, so some of the city's buses were bought last year (II). The city may also have bought diesel or CNG buses last year, so I does not follow.
steps: Electric buses exist and all were bought last year ⇒ II
'All electric buses were bought last year' does not reverse to 'all buses bought last year are electric' ⇒ I fails
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both reverse an 'all' statement.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A survey of 200 visitors at a book fair found that 120 of them bought at least one book.

Conclusions:
I. Most people in the city buy books.
II. The book fair will be held again next year.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The survey covers only 200 fair visitors, who are not a sample of the whole city, so I does not follow. Nothing in the statement concerns future fairs, so II does not follow.
steps: 120 of 200 visitors (60%) bought a book — a fact about the visitors only
I generalises to the whole city ⇒ does not follow
II is a prediction ⇒ does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options accept a generalisation or a prediction that the data cannot support.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The ATM at the railway station dispenses only ₹500 notes, and its limit is ₹20,000 per card per day.

Conclusions:
I. A customer cannot withdraw ₹1,200 from this ATM in a single withdrawal.
II. A customer cannot withdraw more than ₹20,000 in a day from this ATM with one card.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: With only ₹500 notes, every withdrawal is a multiple of ₹500, and ₹1,200 is not, so I follows. The daily limit of ₹20,000 per card gives II directly.
steps: Only ₹500 notes ⇒ amounts in multiples of 500 ⇒ ₹1,200 impossible: I
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I or Only II misses one of two direct consequences; Neither ignores both.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The committee will meet on exactly one day next week, and that day will be either Monday or Tuesday.

Conclusions:
I. The committee will meet on Monday next week.
II. The committee will meet on Tuesday next week.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Either conclusion I or II follows

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The statement does not say which day, so neither conclusion is certain by itself. But the meeting is on exactly one of the two days, so one of the conclusions must be true: either I or II follows.
steps: Exactly one meeting day, Monday or Tuesday
I alone and II alone are not certain
I and II cannot both be false, and cannot both be true ⇒ Either I or II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Either' replaces 'Both' (four-option rule); 'Neither' ignores that one of the two must hold.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Either conclusion I or II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: A train covered 360 km in exactly 4 hours without stopping.

Conclusions:
I. The train's average speed for the journey was 90 km/h.
II. At some moment during the journey, the train's speed was at least 90 km/h.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Average speed = 360 ÷ 4 = 90 km/h, so I follows. If the speed had stayed below 90 km/h the whole time, the train would have covered less than 360 km in 4 hours, so at some moment it must have reached at least 90 km/h (II).
steps: Always below 90 km/h ⇒ distance < 360 km, a contradiction ⇒ II
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I misses that a speed can never stay below its own average throughout; Only II and Neither ignore the direct calculation.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Many passengers at a railway station miss train announcements because the loudspeakers on two platforms are not working.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Stop making announcements at the station
Repair or replace the faulty loudspeakers and show train information on display screens
Ask passengers to reach the station three hours early

solution.concept: A course of action must remove the stated cause
solution.explanation: The cause is broken loudspeakers. Repairing them, with screens as a back-up, solves the problem directly.
steps: Cause: faulty loudspeakers on two platforms
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping announcements worsens the problem; arriving early does not help passengers hear; closing platforms is extreme.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Repair or replace the faulty loudspeakers and show train information on display screens

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A bakery sold 400 loaves of bread in the first week of a month and 500 loaves in the second week, at the same price per loaf in both weeks.

Which of the following can be inferred?

options.text: More customers visited the bakery in the second week
The bakery earned more from selling loaves in the second week than in the first
The bakery will sell 600 loaves in the third week
The bakery's bread became tastier in the second week

solution.concept: Inference: only what the figures guarantee
solution.explanation: Same price per loaf and 100 more loaves sold means higher revenue from loaves in the second week.
steps: Same price, 500 > 400 ⇒ higher revenue in week 2
solution.why_others_wrong: The same customers may simply have bought more; the third-week figure is a prediction; taste is not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The bakery earned more from selling loaves in the second week than in the first

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Claim: Planting a thick row of trees along the school's boundary wall will reduce the noise from the nearby highway inside the classrooms.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

options.text: The highway was widened two years ago
Trees give shade to students during break time
Studies show that a dense belt of trees reduces the traffic noise reaching buildings behind it
Some parents have offered to donate saplings

solution.concept: Strengthen: support the cause–effect link in the claim
solution.explanation: The claim links a row of trees to less noise. Evidence that tree belts reduce traffic noise behind them supports that link directly.
steps: Claim: trees → less highway noise in classrooms
Strengthener: evidence that tree belts block traffic noise
solution.why_others_wrong: Shade and donated saplings do not bear on noise; the widening of the highway explains the noise, not the remedy.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Studies show that a dense belt of trees reduces the traffic noise reaching buildings behind it

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A juice shop owner says that her sales rose last month because of her new radio advertisement.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens her claim?

options.text: The shop sells twelve flavours of juice
The advertisement was played 50 times during the month
Many people in the city listen to the radio
Last month was the hottest month of the year, and sales at juice shops all over the city rose by about the same amount

solution.concept: Weaken: another cause for the same effect
solution.explanation: If juice sales rose equally at shops that did not advertise, the hot weather explains the rise, not the advertisement.
steps: Alternative: a heatwave raised sales everywhere
solution.why_others_wrong: The number of plays and radio listenership, if anything, support the claim; the number of flavours is irrelevant.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Last month was the hottest month of the year, and sales at juice shops all over the city rose by about the same amount

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Every monsoon, several students of a village school fall ill after drinking water from the school's water tank, which has not been cleaned for months.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Remove the water tank without providing another source of water
Close the school for the whole monsoon
Ban students from drinking water at school
Clean the tank regularly and test the drinking water before use

solution.concept: A course of action should fix the cause without causing new harm
solution.explanation: The illnesses come from an uncleaned tank, so regular cleaning and water testing remove the cause.
steps: Remedy: clean it regularly; test the water
solution.why_others_wrong: Closing the school or removing water does not solve the problem and harms the students.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Clean the tank regularly and test the drinking water before use

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a class of 40 students, every student plays at least one of the two games, cricket and football. 25 students play cricket and 22 play football.

Which of the following must be true?

solution.concept: Two overlapping groups that cover everyone
solution.explanation: Since every student plays at least one game, both = 25 + 22 − 40 = 7. Then only cricket = 25 − 7 = 18 and only football = 22 − 7 = 15.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'No student plays both' would give only 47 > 40 places; 17 and 10 are not the correct 'only' counts (18 and 15).
solution.final_answer: Option A: Exactly 7 students play both games

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: Customers of a bank branch complain that they have to stand in a long queue at the counter just to get their passbooks updated.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Close the branch on its busiest days
Stop issuing passbooks to all customers
Allow passbooks to be updated only once a year
Install a self-service passbook printing machine at the branch

solution.concept: A course of action should be practical and aimed at the problem
solution.explanation: The queue forms because passbook updates go through the counter. A self-service printer removes that load from the counter.
steps: Cause: passbook updates at the counter
solution.why_others_wrong: The other steps cut the service itself or make it worse instead of removing the queue.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Install a self-service passbook printing machine at the branch

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: The town should start a weekly farmers' market, because it will let farmers earn more by selling directly to buyers.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

options.text: The town has a large open ground near the bus stand
In nearby towns with weekly farmers' markets, farmers get about 30% more for the same produce than they get from middlemen
Some middlemen oppose the idea of a farmers' market
Many townspeople enjoy shopping on weekends

solution.concept: Strengthen: evidence for the claimed benefit
solution.explanation: The argument's key claim is that direct selling raises farmers' earnings. Evidence from comparable towns that farmers get more at such markets supports exactly that.
steps: Claim: farmers' market → higher farmer earnings
Strengthener: comparable towns show a 30% higher price
solution.why_others_wrong: Weekend shopping and an open ground make the market feasible but do not show higher earnings; middlemen's opposition does not prove a benefit to farmers.
solution.final_answer: Option B: In nearby towns with weekly farmers' markets, farmers get about 30% more for the same produce than they get from middlemen

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A gym claims that its new 12-week programme helps members lose weight, because members who completed the programme lost 6 kg on average.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the claim?

options.text: Members who completed the programme were very satisfied with it
The gym charges a higher fee for the programme
The programme includes three sessions a week
Most members who joined the programme dropped out in the first month, and only those who were already losing weight steadily completed it

solution.concept: Weaken: the result may come from who was counted, not from the programme
solution.explanation: If only members who were already losing weight finished, the 6 kg average describes a self-selected group. The figure cannot show that the programme caused the loss.
steps: Evidence: completers lost 6 kg on average
Weakener: completers were a self-selected group already losing weight
solution.why_others_wrong: Sessions per week and fees do not bear on the result; satisfaction is not evidence of weight loss.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Most members who joined the programme dropped out in the first month, and only those who were already losing weight steadily completed it

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: A city gets all its water from two lakes, A and B. Last year each lake supplied half of the city's water. This year lake A supplied 60% of the water, and the total supply was the same as last year.

Which of the following can be inferred?

options.text: Lake B supplied less water this year than last year
Lake A will supply 70% of the water next year
The city's demand for water fell this year

solution.explanation: With the total unchanged, lake B's share fell from 50% to 40%, so it supplied less water than last year.
steps: Lake B: 50% → 40% of the same total ⇒ less water
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage gives no reason for the change (drying up is a guess); demand is not mentioned and the total supply did not change; next year's share is a prediction.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Lake B supplied less water this year than last year

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Since the city started a free bus service for women, the number of women travelling by bus has risen by 40%. So the free service has increased the number of trips that women in the city make.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The free service costs the city a large amount every year
Many men have asked for free bus travel as well
Most of the new women bus riders earlier made the same trips by auto-rickshaw or shared taxi, and the total number of trips made by women in the city has not changed
Buses on some routes have become crowded during peak hours

solution.concept: Weaken: the evidence shows a shift between modes, not more trips
solution.explanation: The conclusion is about the number of trips, but the evidence is about bus ridership. If the new riders only switched from other modes and total trips are unchanged, the conclusion fails.
steps: Weakener: riders switched modes; total trips unchanged
solution.why_others_wrong: Crowding, men's demands and the cost of the scheme do not bear on whether women make more trips.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Most of the new women bus riders earlier made the same trips by auto-rickshaw or shared taxi, and the total number of trips made by women in the city has not changed

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Passage: This year, the total deposits of Bank X rose by 8%. Its current-account deposits rose by 20%, and all its other deposits together rose by 5%.

Which of the following must be true?

options.text: The share of current-account deposits in total deposits fell this year
This year, current-account deposits are larger than all other deposits together
The bank's other deposits fell this year
Last year, current-account deposits made up exactly 20% of the bank's total deposits

solution.concept: Weighted average of two growth rates
solution.explanation: Let last year's current-account deposits be C and other deposits O. Then 0.20C + 0.05O = 0.08(C + O), so 0.12C = 0.03O and O = 4C. Current-account deposits were C ÷ 5C = 20% of the total.
solution.why_others_wrong: This year current deposits are 1.2C against 4.2C of others; other deposits rose by 5%; the current-account share rose (it grew faster than the total).
solution.final_answer: Option D: Last year, current-account deposits made up exactly 20% of the bank's total deposits

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: An audit found that many names on a district's ration-card list belong to people who died or moved away years ago, while several needy families in the district have no ration card.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Verify the list door to door, remove ineligible names and enrol the needy families who were left out
Take no action, since most cards on the list are genuine
Stop the ration scheme in the district
Cancel all ration cards and issue no new ones

solution.concept: A course of action should fix both errors without hurting eligible people
solution.explanation: There are two problems: ineligible names on the list and eligible families left out. Door-to-door verification with removal and fresh enrolment fixes both while keeping the scheme for genuine beneficiaries.
steps: Remedy: verify, remove and enrol — the scheme continues for genuine holders
solution.why_others_wrong: Stopping the scheme or cancelling all cards punishes genuine beneficiaries; doing nothing leaves both problems in place.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Verify the list door to door, remove ineligible names and enrol the needy families who were left out

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A restaurant chain claims that its new online ordering system, and not any price cut, raised its orders by 25% over the last six months.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the claim?

options.text: The chain did not change its prices in the last six months, and its outlets that had not yet adopted the system saw no rise in orders
Customers often say they like discounts
The online system cost the chain a large amount to build
Orders at rival restaurant chains also rose by about 25% in the same period

solution.concept: Strengthen: rule out the alternative and compare with a control group
solution.explanation: Unchanged prices rule out the price explanation, and outlets without the system seeing no rise point to the system as the cause of the increase.
steps: Claim: ordering system (not prices) → 25% more orders
No price change ⇒ the price explanation is ruled out
Outlets without the system: no rise ⇒ supports the system as the cause
solution.why_others_wrong: A similar rise at rivals points to a market-wide cause and weakens the claim; liking discounts and the system's cost do not bear on the cause of the rise.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The chain did not change its prices in the last six months, and its outlets that had not yet adopted the system saw no rise in orders

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what service do bees provide to crops?

options.text: They feed on the pests that attack fruit and vegetable crops.
They improve the quality of the soil in which the plants grow.
They carry pollen between flowers, which helps the plants produce fruit.
They shade young plants from the strong heat of the sun.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says crops depend on bees 'to carry pollen from one flower to another', and that without this service many plants would produce fewer and smaller fruits, or none at all.
steps: Without it, fewer fruits: option C
solution.why_others_wrong: Eating pests (A), improving soil (B) and shading plants (D) are never mentioned as things bees do.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They carry pollen between flowers, which helps the plants produce fruit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following does the passage mention as a likely reason why wild bees are becoming harder to find?

options.text: Spraying pesticides at times when bees are active
Farmers harvesting too much honey from wild hives
Unusually cold winters in farming areas
Too many bee boxes placed at the edges of fields

solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 names two likely reasons: the loss of hedges and wild plants at field edges, and 'the careless spraying of pesticides at times when bees are active'.
steps: Find 'wild bees are becoming harder to find' in paragraph 2
Reasons given: loss of hedges; careless spraying
Option A matches the second reason
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are not mentioned. D reverses the passage: bee boxes are a response by farmers, not a cause of the decline.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Spraying pesticides at times when bees are active

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, may a beekeeper find it hard to earn a fair price for her honey?

options.text: Honey spoils quickly in hot weather and cannot be stored for long.
Fake honey drags prices down, and she may be unable to show that hers is pure.
Universities buy most of the honey from beekeepers at a fixed, very low price.
Most people in India prefer sugar to honey and buy very little of it.

solution.concept: Inference: linking two sentences in the same paragraph
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says cheap, adulterated products 'pull down the price for genuine producers', and a beekeeper 'who cannot prove the purity of her honey may find it hard to earn a fair price'.
steps: Problem 1: cheap, adulterated honey lowers prices
Problem 2: genuine producers must prove purity
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are not stated anywhere. Universities offer training, not a market for honey.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Fake honey drags prices down, and she may be unable to show that hers is pure.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'modest' as used in the passage ('the cost of starting is modest compared with most other farm businesses')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: modest (of an amount) = not large
solution.explanation: The sentence compares the cost of starting beekeeping with that of other farm businesses and presents it as an advantage. Here 'modest' describes an amount, so it means small or moderate.
steps: 'modest' here describes a cost, not a person
Presented as an advantage → the cost is low
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Shy' is a meaning of 'modest' only when it describes a person. 'Enormous' is the opposite. 'Boastful' is the opposite of the personal sense of 'modest'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How to Make Honey at Home

solution.concept: A title must cover the main idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage explains how much crops depend on bees, why wild bees are declining, how keeping bees helps farmers and what difficulties it brings, ending with the idea that bees are 'living helpers that ask for little'.
steps: Para 1: bees pollinate crops for free
Paras 2–4: decline of wild bees; beekeeping and its problems
Para 5: bees as helpers of the farm: option A
solution.why_others_wrong: B is not discussed. C picks up only the opening remark about stings. D goes beyond the passage, which criticises careless spraying but never calls for a ban.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Bees: The Farmer's Unpaid Helpers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why did Kamala Devi keep her new smartphone in its box for three months?

options.text: The phone did not work properly in her area, where the signal was weak.
She feared losing money by a wrong press and did not want to trouble her grandchildren.
Her son had asked her not to use it until he could show her how.
She could not afford to pay the monthly charges for a connection.

solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 gives two reasons: she 'was afraid of pressing the wrong button and losing money', and she 'did not want to keep asking her busy grandchildren for help'.
steps: Find 'kept it in its box' in paragraph 1
Read the next sentence: fear of losing money; not wanting to trouble her grandchildren
solution.why_others_wrong: A, C and D are not mentioned. The passage gives only the two reasons in option B.
solution.final_answer: Option B: She feared losing money by a wrong press and did not want to trouble her grandchildren.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as something taught in the classes?

options.text: Enlarging the text on the screen

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists making a video call, reading a message and booking a doctor's appointment, and adds enlarging the text and typing by speaking. Opening a bank account is not mentioned.
steps: Also: enlarging the text (C), typing by speaking
Opening a bank account is not listed: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the 'NOT mentioned' answer. Bank accounts appear only in paragraph 2, where pensions are credited to them.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Opening a new bank account

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to Kamala Devi, what helped her most in learning to use her phone?

options.text: The patience of the young volunteer who taught her
The printed instruction book that came with the phone
The low price of the phone

solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says what helped her most 'was not the technology itself but the patience of the young volunteer who taught her'.
steps: Find 'What helped her most' in paragraph 4
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C are never mentioned. D contradicts the passage: at home 'everyone was in a hurry', and she did not want to keep asking her grandchildren.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The patience of the young volunteer who taught her

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest by saying that such a class 'can close other gaps too'?

options.text: The classes also help older people save money on their bills.
The classes bring young and old people closer to each other.
The classes reduce the gap between rich and poor towns.
The classes close the gap between what phones cost and what people earn.

solution.concept: Inference: what a closing remark refers to
solution.explanation: The sentence before it says the young volunteers had rarely spent time with people of their grandparents' age and discover 'stories, advice and humour' they had not expected. The other gap closed is the one between generations.
steps: Context: volunteers learn from the elderly learners
Gap besides the digital one: between generations
solution.why_others_wrong: Money saved (A), rich and poor towns (C) and the cost of phones (D) are not discussed in the last paragraph.
solution.final_answer: Option B: The classes bring young and old people closer to each other.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'bear' as used in the passage ('the loss of independence is harder to bear than the inconvenience')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: bear = endure, put up with
solution.explanation: Something 'hard to bear' is hard to endure or put up with. The passage says losing independence is harder to tolerate than the inconvenience itself.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Carry' and 'hold up' are physical senses of 'bear', and 'produce' is the sense in 'bear fruit'. None fits a feeling that is hard to put up with.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how can traffic noise at night harm a person's health even if it does not fully wake him?

options.text: It damages his hearing, and hearing loss over years is linked to heart disease.
It disturbs his sleep, and poor sleep over years is linked to high blood pressure and heart disease.
It lowers his concentration, and he scores worse on reading tests the next day.
It forces him to take sleeping pills, which over time raise his blood pressure.
